l: Acontius, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Acontius has bound the speaker through a written oath and caused her to be struck by a distant, letter-like wound. He wishes to visit her, is urged to pray for her recovery, and is finally told that she wishes to be united with him.

l: Cydippe, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: The speaker has become ill whenever preparations for marriage are made and has seen Hymenaeus flee from her wedding ceremonies three times. She rejects her intended husband, confesses her feelings to Acontius, admits that she wants to join him, and tells her mother about the oath.

l: Diana, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Diana is regarded by the speaker as the goddess whose anger has caused her bodily illness and prevented her marriages. The speaker asks Diana to spare her and obtain the healing aid of her brother.

l: Acontius's apple, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Acontius’s apple carried the writing through which the speaker was deceived into accepting the oath. The speaker compares its bloodless color with the pallor of her own sick body.

l: the written oath, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: The written oath has bound the speaker despite her lack of genuine consent and has become the basis of her conflict with Acontius. She eventually yields to it and tells her mother about the pledge her tongue was trapped into giving.

l: Acontius's letter, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Acontius’s letter wounds the speaker from afar like a dart and contributes to her illness. She nevertheless uses her own letter to confess her feelings and communicate that she wants to be united with him.

l: Cydippe's illness, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: The illness leaves the speaker fevered, weak, wasted, bloodless, and pale. It repeatedly appears when marriage rites are prepared, and the speaker seeks divine help to recover.

l: the intended husband, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: The intended husband sits beside the speaker as much as he is permitted but respects the virginity of their bed. He becomes suspicious because she turns away from him, rejects his touch, avoids speaking, and refuses his kisses.

l: marriage bed, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Marriage preparations have been made for the speaker three times, but each ceremony has failed when her illness and fear of death appear. The speaker ultimately presents union with Acontius as the remaining course.

l: Ovid, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: Ovid is identified by the surrounding editorial material as the author whose Heroides and Amores are being presented. The unit’s discussion describes the Amores as generally light, elegant, playful, and shaped by poetic art rather than profound personal emotion.

l: The Amores, Heroides and Amores, Cum tamen haec dixi, cum me tibi firma negavi,
s: The Amores section provides information about its principal manuscripts, early editions, and modern editions. Its introduction characterizes the poems as largely lighthearted love poetry, while noting that they also reflect ancient Roman and Italian life.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: P. Ovidius Naso presents the Amores as a reduced collection of three books and begins by describing how Cupid redirected his intended epic poetry into elegy. The speaker acknowledges that Cupid has wounded him and submits to Love, while asking a beloved woman to accept his devotion and inspire his poetry. At a banquet, the speaker anxiously instructs the beloved woman how to communicate secretly and avoid intimacy with her husband. Later, Corinna visits the speaker, removes her clothing after a feigned resistance, and they have sex.

l: P. Ovidius Naso, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: P. Ovidius Naso is identified as the author of the Amores. His work was formerly in five booklets but is now presented in three, because the author preferred this revised form.

l: the poet's Amores, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: The poet's Amores are presented as three booklets rather than five. They contain elegiac love poetry about Cupid, Love, the speaker's beloved woman, and Corinna.

l: Love (Amor), Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: Cupid interrupts the speaker's attempt to compose epic poetry by stealing a metrical foot and changing the work into elegy. He shoots the speaker with an arrow, claims the speaker as his new prey, and is imagined as a victorious deity proceeding in a triumph with captives and attendants.

l: Corinna, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: Corinna visits the speaker during the hot midday and appears in a loosely fastened tunic with her hair covering her neck. The speaker removes her tunic; after resisting in a way that appears unwilling, she is overcome, and they have sex before resting together.

l: the speaker's beloved woman's husband, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: The beloved woman's husband attends the same banquet as the speaker and the woman. The speaker fears his physical intimacy with her, instructs her to avoid his embraces and kisses, and hopes that wine will make him sleep so that the lovers can find an opportunity to meet.

l: Love, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: Love takes possession of the speaker's heart and torments him after Cupid's arrow strikes. The speaker says that resisting Love makes its pressure worse, while accepting its service makes the burden lighter.

l: love poetry, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: The speaker abandons the preparation of violent epic poetry for lighter elegiac verse when Cupid alters his meter. Love poetry is presented as deriving its subject from the beloved woman, whose beauty and relationship with the speaker can make their names famous throughout the world.

l: Venus, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: Venus is invoked as the deity who may hear the speaker's prayers that the beloved woman either love him or at least allow herself to be loved. She is also contrasted with Minerva in the speaker's argument that gods should not exchange their characteristic powers.

l: the husband-wife banquet, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: The husband-wife banquet brings the speaker, the beloved woman, and her husband together. The speaker gives the woman covert instructions involving touches, looks, gestures, cups, wine, and the crowd, while warning her not to show affection to her husband.

l: Cupid's triumph, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: Cupid's triumph is imagined as a public victory procession in which Modesty and other obstacles to Love are led captive. Cupid rides in a golden chariot drawn by his mother's doves, while roses, jewels, attendants, captive youths, captive girls, and the speaker himself form part of the spectacle.

l: the speaker's submission to Cupid, Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS AMORES / LIBER PRIMUS
s: The speaker confesses that he is Cupid's new prey and stretches out his hands to accept Cupid's laws. He asks for peace rather than war and accepts that his poetry must rise in six-foot lines and settle into five-foot lines.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The unit concerns a lover who spends the night begging a janitor to open a barred door so that he may reach his mistress. Love gives the lover courage to move secretly at night, but the janitor repeatedly refuses, and the lover's pleas, threats, and appeals to past gratitude fail. The lover then blames anger and violence against the mistress, regretting that he struck and disfigured her before begging forgiveness. At dawn, he remains remorseful and asks that his own hands be punished.

The janitor is bound by a hard chain and refuses to open the door for the lover despite repeated pleas, appeals to gratitude, and threats. The lover calls him harder than the door and says he is more suited to guarding a gloomy prison than the mistress's threshold.

The lover secretly approaches the door at night, carrying only Love, some wine, and a fallen garland as companions. He repeatedly begs the janitor to admit him, threatens to attack the house, and finally leaves in anger and shame after the door remains closed. He also admits that he violently struck his mistress and deeply regrets it.

The mistress is the lover's beloved and is inside the house whose door he cannot enter. In the later episode, she is frightened and wounded when the lover tears her hair and marks her cheeks, but she remains silent while her tears and expression accuse him.
Cupid, together with his mother, laughs at the lover's former fear of night and promises that he will become brave. Love then remains with the lover as he approaches the guarded door.

The door remains closed and rigid despite the lover's tears, prayers, threats, and appeals. The lover briefly thinks that it has moved on its hinge, but discovers that the sound came only from the wind; he ends by cursing and bidding farewell to the door and its posts.

l: door bar, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The lover repeatedly orders the door bar to be removed before the night ends. It remains in place, braced by hard oak, and prevents him from entering.

The chain binds the janitor, and the lover wishes that the janitor may eventually be freed from it and no longer have to drink the water of slavery. The chain is also invoked as a possible punishment for the lover's own violent hands.

The night initially frightens the lover with darkness and empty phantoms, but Love makes him brave enough to travel and keep watch at the door. As the hours pass, the city becomes silent, dew falls, and dawn approaches while the door remains shut.
Anger makes the lover its prey and drives him to raise reckless hands against his mistress. Afterward, he recognizes that he used his strength against her and condemns his own anger.

l: violence against the mistress, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The lover tears the mistress's hair from her brow and marks her free-born cheeks with his nails after shouting threats and pulling apart her gown. She becomes bloodless and trembles, and her tears make the lover realize that he has committed a crime.

l: the lover's vigil at the door, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The lover spends the night outside the closed door, repeatedly calling for the bar to be removed and listening for signs that the door has opened. He sheds tears, wears a garland that falls from his hair, and remains outside until the approach of dawn, when he leaves the garland on the threshold as evidence of his miserable vigil.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VIII
s: Dipsas, an old bawd skilled in magic, counsels a young woman on how to attract and exploit wealthy lovers. She tells the young woman to use feigned modesty, rivalry, tears, deception, and repeated demands for gifts and payment. The narrator and poet-lover overhears the speech while hidden behind doors and nearly attacks Dipsas in anger. Dipsas presents the wealthy young lover as a desirable source of money, while dismissing the narrator's poetry as inadequate compensation.

Dipsas is an old bawd whose name reflects her thirst, and she is also portrayed as a practitioner of magic. She knows incantations, herbs, magical devices, and poisons, can summon the dead, alter the weather, change form, and fly at night. She counsels the young woman to pursue wealthy lovers through deception, rivalry, feigned emotion, and demands for gifts, and the narrator overhears her.

The narrator and poet-lover hides behind double doors and overhears Dipsas advising the young woman. He is angered when Dipsas asks what he gives besides new poems and nearly attacks her, but restrains himself; he ends by wishing her poverty, thirst, and a miserable old age.

The young woman has attracted the attention of a wealthy young lover and blushes when Dipsas tells her so. Dipsas urges her to exploit her beauty by pretending modesty, refusing and accepting favors strategically, cultivating rivals, displaying signs of other lovers, and securing gifts through herself and her household.

l: the wealthy young lover, Heroides and Amores, VIII
s: The wealthy young lover has been captivated by the young woman's face and desires her. Dipsas says that he has concern for what she lacks and urges her to make him pay for access while keeping him uncertain and jealous.
Mars is said by Dipsas to have previously opposed the young woman through an unfavorable star. Dipsas says that Mars has now departed, leaving Venus favorably placed.

Venus is said to rule in the city of Aeneas and to favor the young woman after Mars has departed. Dipsas invokes Venus to justify deception in love, claiming that Venus turns a deaf ear to false oaths and permits such tricks in play.

l: gifts and payment for sexual favors, Heroides and Amores, VIII
s: Dipsas teaches the young woman to demand gifts and payment while pretending love, to admit lovers according to what they bring, and to use slaves, a sister, a mother, and a nurse to solicit additional gifts. She recommends birthday pretexts, presents from rivals, and even asking for a loan that will never be repaid; the narrator's poetry is treated as insufficient payment.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: The unit compares the lover with the soldier, presenting both as sleepless, enduring, watchful, and capable of overcoming danger for the sake of love or war. It says that love is not idleness and that the lover is driven to action by Venus and by the beloved. It then contrasts unbought love with love sought for payment, arguing that Venus, sexual pleasure, and gifts should not be treated as commercial transactions. The speaker condemns women who demand payment while allowing gifts from wealthy lovers and praises the poor lover's service, devotion, and poetry.
Cupid has a camp of his own, and every lover serves as a soldier in it.

The lover is compared to a soldier because he keeps watch through the night, endures cold, rain, snow, mountains, rivers, and sea travel, watches a rival as though he were an enemy, and besieges a beloved's threshold. Love drives the formerly idle speaker into action, and the lover is said to be suited to anyone ready for trials.

The soldier serves in a camp, keeps watch through the night, rests on the ground, scouts dangerous enemies, besieges cities, breaks gates, and endures difficult journeys and weather. His courage and endurance are presented as qualities also sought by the beloved in a lover.

Love is presented as active rather than idle, requiring an experienced and energetic spirit. It can make people endure hardship, inspire warriors, and cause a person formerly devoted to leisure to enter another's camp.

War is compared with love through their shared dangers, sleeplessness, watchfulness, sieges, attacks, and uncertain outcomes. The unit says that both war and love can bring down people who seemed impossible to defeat, while the defeated may rise again.
Venus is associated with the age suited to warfare and with the camp of love. Neither Venus nor her son is suited to earning the pay of soldiers, because they are unwarlike gods.

The harlot is described as available to anyone for a fixed payment and as seeking gains through her body when commanded. Even so, she curses the authority of the greedy pander and performs for compulsion what others do willingly.

The woman is criticized for being the only creature said to demand payment for mutual sexual pleasure, to hire out her nights, and to profit from what both partners desire. The unit nevertheless says that a woman may properly request gifts from a wealthy person and that a poor lover should give whatever he has, including service, devotion, faithfulness, and poetry.

The man is presented as contributing to sexual pleasure together with the woman, yet being made to suffer a financial loss when the woman demands payment. A poor man is said to offer his service, devotion, faithfulness, and whatever possessions he has to his beloved.

l: sexual pleasure, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Sexual pleasure is described as something that man and woman both enjoy and jointly produce. Because it is mutual, the unit questions why one person should sell it and the other should have to buy it.

l: gifts and payment for sexual favors, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Payment for love is condemned as degrading, because paying in full releases the recipient from any remaining obligation. Gifts are treated differently when they are freely given, especially by a wealthy person, while a poor lover is encouraged to give service, devotion, faithfulness, or poetry; such poetry can provide enduring fame after clothes, jewels, and gold have been destroyed.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, XI
s: Naso asks Nape to deliver wax tablets to Corinna and ensure that she reads and answers them promptly. Nape is described as skilled in arranging hair, serving during secret nighttime activities, and giving signals, and as someone who has often helped Naso. The message says that Naso lives in hope of a night with Corinna and asks her to come. Naso would dedicate the tablets to Venus if Corinna wrote only “Come!” in reply.

Nape is skilled at arranging scattered locks and is useful in secret nighttime activities and in giving signals. She has often urged Corinna to come to Naso and has proved faithful to Naso in difficulties. Naso asks her to deliver his inscribed tablets to Corinna, remove delays, observe Corinna’s reaction, and make sure she replies.

Naso sends Corinna a message saying that he lives through hope of a night with her. He asks Nape to secure Corinna’s prompt reply and says he would dedicate the tablets to Venus as faithful aids if Corinna answered only “Come!”

Corinna is Nape’s mistress and the intended recipient of Naso’s tablets. She has previously hesitated about coming to Naso, and Naso asks Nape to watch her face as she reads and to make her write a substantial reply without delay.

l: wax tablets, Heroides and Amores, XI
s: The wax tablets are inscribed by Naso and carried by Nape to Corinna. Naso wants Corinna to fill them with a reply, but says that a single word, “Come!”, would be enough; he would then dedicate the tablets to Venus.
The message tells Corinna that Naso remains alive through hope of a night with her and that the rest of his feelings are written in the wax. It asks her to come and to answer promptly.

l: secret nighttime meeting, Heroides and Amores, XI
s: Nape is known for her usefulness in the service of a secret nighttime meeting and for giving signals. She has often encouraged Corinna to come to Naso, but the unit does not state that the meeting occurs.

l: love correspondence, Heroides and Amores, XI
s: Naso’s love correspondence with Corinna is carried through Nape and written on wax tablets. Naso wants Corinna’s written response to occupy the tablets rather than leave them largely blank, though he would accept the single-word reply “Come!”

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The speaker laments tablets that return from the beloved woman bearing a refusal, then curses the tablets and the tree from which they were made. He reproaches Aurora for ending his night with the beloved, while praising the pleasures of sleep and intimacy. He mourns the beloved woman’s damaged hair, attributes its loss to her own treatment, and consoles her that it can be replaced. Finally, he defends poetry against Envy, claiming that poetic fame outlasts rulers, monuments, and death.

l: P. Ovidius Naso, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The speaker is distressed when the tablets return with the message that meeting the beloved woman is impossible that day. He reproaches Aurora for arriving too soon, consoles the beloved woman over her damaged hair, and declares that his poetry will preserve him after death.

The beloved woman sends tablets bearing a refusal, and she once stopped at the threshold after striking her toe. She has lost her formerly abundant, delicate hair through her own treatment of it, and she blushes and weeps while looking at the severed hair.

l: wax tablets, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The tablets return with gloomy news that the beloved woman cannot come that day. The speaker calls them ill-natured, funereal, and double in their dealings, throws curses upon them, and wishes them to decay or be crushed.

Aurora comes over the ocean from her aged husband and brings the day in a golden chariot. The speaker begs her to delay, accusing her of disturbing lovers, waking workers and students, and leaving her aged husband for disliked morning duties.

l: the dawn, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The dawn ends the speaker’s night with the beloved woman even though sleep is still deep, the air cool, and the birds singing. Its arrival wakes travelers, soldiers, farmers, boys, lawyers, and women who work wool.

l: the hair, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The beloved woman’s former hair was abundant, delicate, easily arranged, and a mixture of black and golden color. It endured irons and fire but was ultimately ruined by her own dyes and treatments; the speaker says that replacement hair from captive German women will be sent.

Envy accuses the speaker of wasting his vigorous years and producing poetry instead of pursuing military prizes or legal work. The speaker says that Envy feeds on the living but becomes quiet after death.

l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: The speaker claims that poetry survives longer than rocks, ploughs, kings, triumphs, gold, and monuments. He says that the works of Homer, Hesiod, Callimachus, Sophocles, Aratus, Menander, Ennius, Accius, Lucretius, Virgil, Tibullus, and Gallus will endure, and that his own poetry will survive him.
Death is presented as unable to destroy poetry or the fame preserved by song. The speaker says that even after the final fire consumes him, a large part of him will continue to live.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Ovid presents himself as a poet of love whose elegies are composed at Amor’s command and intended for lovers. He recalls abandoning grand epic subjects when his beloved mistress closed her door, after which song softened the barrier and brought her to him. He urges the mistress’s guardian to permit a discreet affair, arguing that secrecy will benefit the guardian and that jealous surveillance harms everyone. He also confesses that he is attracted to women of every kind and cannot control his continual inclination to love.

l: Ovid, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Ovid identifies himself as Naso, born among the Paeligni and a poet of his own disreputable ways. He says that he lacks the strength and will to govern himself, is drawn to women for countless reasons, and cannot stop being what he hates.

l: Love, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Amor commands Ovid to compose the present elegies and dictates his songs. Ovid presents himself as wounded by Amor’s bow and guided by Amor toward love poetry rather than epic subjects.

l: the beloved mistress, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: The beloved mistress closes her door to Ovid, causing him to abandon his thunderbolt imagery and return to elegy. Her beauty and favor reward his poetry, and a beloved woman eventually comes to the poet in response to his praise.

l: the mistress's guardian, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: The mistress’s guardian, addressed as Bagoas, prevents Ovid from safely approaching the woman. Ovid urges him to stop earning hatred, accept gifts for keeping silent, and allow secret meetings, warning that a guardian who reveals an affair may be punished.

l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Song and poetry are portrayed as powerful enough to bring down the moon, recall the sun’s horses, silence serpents, reverse flowing water, and overcome barred doors. Ovid says that his elegies soften the mistress’s door and win him a greater reward than singing of heroic figures would.

l: adultery, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Ovid seeks the guardian’s help so that he and the mistress can love safely and discreetly. The proposed affair relies on false explanations, concealed messages, invented visits, and the guardian’s silence rather than violence or poison.

l: jealous guardianship, Heroides and Amores, LIBER SECUNDUS
s: Excessive guardianship is presented as provoking hatred and making illicit love more desirable. Ovid argues that surveillance damages the husband, mistress, and guardian, while a guardian who keeps silent gains influence, rewards, and eventual freedom.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, V
s: The speaker/lover accuses the beloved girl of infidelity after secretly watching her exchange coded signals and kisses with another man at a drinking party. He angrily claims that her kisses belong to him and asks why a third person shares them. When the girl blushes, looks down, and appears sorrowful, his anger collapses into supplication, and he begs her for kisses. Her new kisses please and torment him because he suspects another man taught her how to give them.

l: P. Ovidius Naso, Heroides and Amores, V
s: The speaker/lover believes the beloved girl has been unfaithful after observing her hidden communication and kissing another man. He initially threatens to assert his rights and is moved to attack her, but her ashamed and sorrowful appearance disarms him; he then begs for kisses and becomes jealous that another man may have enjoyed them.

l: beloved girl, Heroides and Amores, V
s: The beloved girl communicates secretly through gestures, looks, writing on the table, and coded speech, then kisses another man after the other guests have left. When confronted, she blushes, looks at the ground, and appears sorrowful before giving the speaker/lover exceptionally pleasing kisses.

Love is presented as so painful that the speaker/lover often prays for death. The speaker/lover still treats the beloved girl’s kisses as a shared possession and cannot bear a third person enjoying them.
The speaker/lover says that death is often the subject of his prayers because the pain caused by love and the beloved girl is so great.

The beloved girl’s infidelity is revealed not by intercepted letters or gifts but by the speaker/lover’s direct observation of her secret signs and kisses with another man. The speaker/lover considers his case against her overwhelmingly strong, yet wishes he could be unable to win it.

Jealousy makes the speaker/lover angry when he sees the beloved girl kissing another man, but it also torments him after she gives him better and seemingly newly learned kisses. He fears that the rival has tasted the same pleasures and wishes the rival’s kisses had not been equally satisfying.

The beloved girl’s kisses with another man are described as intimate and unlike the kisses of a sister and brother. Her later kisses to the speaker/lover are heartfelt, exceptionally powerful, and apparently more skillful than before, suggesting that someone else taught her how to give them.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The unit first mourns the death of Corinna’s parrot, praising its Indian origin, mimicry, loyalty to a turtle-dove, and final cry of “Corinna, vale!” It then presents the speaker’s defenses against Corinna’s jealousy, especially her accusation that he has slept with Cypassis. The speaker later admits that he did have an affair with Cypassis and threatens to reveal its details if she refuses him. The final poems portray Cupid and love as forces that repeatedly restore the speaker’s desire, including his simultaneous love for two women.

The parrot, brought from India, dies after being praised for its rare coloring, red-and-yellow beak, skill at imitating human speech, peaceful nature, and frugal diet. It is mourned by birds and by Corinna, and its dying tongue cries, “Corinna, vale!” It is received among the pious birds in Elysium, where its speech attracts them, and its tombstone says that it pleased its mistress and spoke better than a bird.
The turtle-dove is described as the parrot’s faithful companion. The two lived in complete harmony and remained loyal to the end, so the turtle-dove is urged to grieve before all other birds.

Corinna mourns the parrot and makes vows for its safety, but the vows are carried away by the South Wind. She becomes jealous when the speaker looks at or praises other women and accuses him of desiring Cypassis. The parrot’s last word is her name.

Cypassis is skilled at arranging Corinna’s hair and is described as a faithful servant. Corinna accuses her of sharing her mistress’s couch with the speaker, while the speaker first denies the charge and later addresses Cypassis as a partner in their secret affair. He threatens to tell Corinna where, how often, and in what ways they were together if Cypassis refuses him.

Cupid wounds the speaker even though the speaker has never abandoned Cupid’s standards. The speaker complains that Cupid attacks friends rather than enemies, but he ultimately invites Cupid and his mother to reign permanently in his heart and to rule over the women who are their subjects.

Love leaves the speaker weakened and repeatedly strips him to his bones, although many men and women remain without love. Even when the speaker grows weary and his desire cools, love carries him back like a changing wind and makes him take up its familiar weapons again. He calls love a sweet evil and prefers its uncertain pleasures, including both enjoyment and rejection, to peaceful rest.

l: Cypassis and the speaker's affair, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The affair is a secret sexual relationship between Cypassis and the speaker. Although the speaker denies the accusation when defending himself to Corinna, he later refers openly to their previous encounters and uses knowledge of them to pressure Cypassis into another meeting.

l: two simultaneous love affairs, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The speaker admits that he loves two women at the same time, despite having previously denied that this was possible. He presents this condition as shameful but acknowledges that he has been caught loving both simultaneously.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, X
s: The unit presents the speaker’s divided love for two beautiful women, his preference for a life consumed by erotic love, and his wish to die during its pleasures. It then describes his anxiety over Corinna’s intended sea voyage and his hopes for her safe return. The speaker celebrates gaining Corinna as a triumph achieved without military aid. Finally, he prays for Corinna’s survival during a dangerous pregnancy and condemns abortion as harmful to women and unborn children.

Corinna prepares to leave her familiar bed and household and undertake a dangerous voyage by sea. The speaker hopes she will return safely, welcomes her imagined arrival, and later fears for her life when she undergoes a dangerous attempt to end a pregnancy.

Love divides the speaker between two women, each of whom he finds beautiful and pleasing. He prefers a life troubled and exhausted by love to a solitary life, and he wishes his death to result from erotic love.

l: the sea, Heroides and Amores, X
s: The sea is presented as treacherous, with storms, contrary winds, deep waters, dangerous rocks, Scylla, Charybdis, and the Syrtes. A sailor fears death when the shore recedes and the waves are roughened.

l: the Argo, Heroides and Amores, X
s: The Argo is identified as the first ship to venture through the dangerous sea between the clashing rocks while carrying the golden-fleeced ram. The speaker wishes that it had been overwhelmed so that no one would disturb the open sea with oars.

l: Corinna's voyage, Heroides and Amores, X
s: Corinna's voyage is described as a hazardous departure from her known home over treacherous waters. The speaker fears the winds and storms, urges a safe return, and imagines welcoming her ship, embracing her, and hearing how narrowly she escaped the sea.

l: the triumph, Heroides and Amores, X
s: The speaker claims a triumph because Corinna is in his arms after being guarded by her husband, keeper, and door. He calls it a special victory because it was won without bloodshed or military assistance, with himself serving as commander, soldier, cavalry, infantry, and standard-bearer.

Isis is invoked as a goddess associated with Paraetonium, Canopus, Memphis, Pharos, and the Nile. The speaker prays that she will turn her attention toward Corinna and spare both Corinna and himself by granting Corinna life.

Corinna lies exhausted and in danger while attempting to remove the burden of her pregnant belly. The speaker believes that he may be responsible for the conception and asks Isis and Ilithyia to preserve Corinna's life.

Abortion is condemned as a practice in which women wound themselves and give deadly poisons to unborn children to avoid bodily marks. The speaker warns that women who destroy a pregnancy may themselves die and urges that a pregnancy be allowed to grow until its natural maturity.

l: the unborn children, Heroides and Amores, X
s: The unborn children are described as vulnerable lives harmed by weapons and deadly poisons. The speaker argues that the human race and important figures such as Romulus and Aeneas would never have existed if their mothers had destroyed them before birth.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: The speaker sends a ring to his fair beloved and wishes that she will welcome it, wear it, and feel his love conveyed with it. He imagines becoming the ring so that he could touch her body, remain on her finger, and fall into her bosom. In Sulmo, the Paelignian country is fertile, watered, and healthy, but the speaker finds no comfort there because his beloved is absent. He declares that any journey would be easy with her, while separation makes even his native land seem as harsh as Scythia, Cilicia, Britain, or the rocks stained with Prometheus’s blood.

l: the speaker's beloved, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: The speaker's beloved is to receive and wear the ring as a gift. She is imagined touching her breasts, inserting her left hand into her tunic, bathing while wearing the ring, and using it to seal secret tablets. The speaker urges her to come to him quickly in a small carriage if she cares for him.

The ring is sent to circle the finger of the speaker's fair beloved, carrying the giver's love rather than material value. It is wished to fit her finger well, remain with her during bathing, and help seal her secret letters. The speaker envies the gift and imagines becoming it so that it could touch her lips, fall into her bosom, and act as a man.
Sulmo holds the speaker in the third part of the Paelignian fields. Although it is fertile and watered, it does not satisfy him because his beloved is far away.

l: Ovid's Paelignian homeland, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: The Paelignian country is described as small, healthy, fertile, and rich in flowing water. Its fields produce grass, grain, grapes, and the berry-bearing tree of Pallas, while streams and cool breezes refresh the land. Without the beloved, however, the speaker does not experience it as his healthy native country.

l: the sea voyage and journey, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: The speaker says that a journey with his beloved would be gentle even across the windy Alps, the Libyan Syrtes, and dangerous seas. With her, he would not fear the monsters beneath the maiden's groin, Malea, or Charybdis, and he would carry her if Neptune defeated the ship. The journey of the young man visiting Hero failed only because the way became blind.

l: separation from the beloved, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: Separation places the speaker away from the woman who causes his passion. It makes Sulmo and his father's country seem like Scythia, the fierce Cilicians, the green Britons, and rocks reddened by Promethean blood. The beloved had sworn to remain his companion, but the speaker says that girls' promises are often carried away by wind and water.

l: love and longing, Heroides and Amores, XV
s: The speaker's love is expressed through the gift of the ring and through his wish to become the object that touches and accompanies his beloved. His longing makes him envy his own gift and desire physical closeness with her. He asks her to turn her promises into actions by coming to him.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, XVII
s: The speaker defends serving a beautiful woman and argues that Corinna’s beauty makes her arrogant and haughty. He compares unequal lovers and verse, asking his mistress to accept him on whatever terms she chooses, while declaring that only she will be sung in his books. He explains to Macer that Love has diverted him from epic and tragic poetry toward love poetry and letters. In addressing a husband, he claims that jealousy, refusal, and obstacles strengthen love, and warns that the husband’s excessive tolerance may cause Corinna to cease being his.

The speaker accepts being considered a slave to a woman if her fires consume him less harshly. He presents himself as devoted to his mistress, willing to obey her laws, and dependent on obstacles and jealousy to sustain his love. He tells the husband that excessive tolerance frustrates his own affair and urges him to guard the woman more closely.

Corinna’s beauty is said to make her hard and arrogant with the speaker. She recognizes his susceptibility to refusal and jealousy, feigns illness or wrongdoing, and then becomes affectionate when his desire has been renewed. Another woman is said to publicize that she is Corinna because the speaker’s poetry gives the name distinction.

l: the husband, Heroides and Amores, XVII
s: The husband is criticized for being too slow and tolerant of what no husband should endure. The speaker urges him to close the door at night, investigate visitors and messages, and notice why his wife sleeps apart from him. His indulgence is said to spoil the speaker’s pleasure and may cause the woman to cease being the speaker’s.

Love is presented as a force that triumphs over the speaker’s attempts to undertake epic or tragic subjects. It laughs at his theatrical costume and sceptre, draws him away from tragedy, and leads the buskined poet in triumph. Love is also invoked as the force that makes lesser and greater partners fit together.

Beauty gives people confidence and breeds arrogance. The speaker says that a beautiful face can inspire pride and a promise of rule, but argues that beauty should not lead its possessor to scorn a lesser partner.

Love grows stronger through refusal, fear, delay, and obstacles, while excessive indulgence turns it into something cloying and harmful. The speaker says that he pursues what flees and flees what follows him, and he wishes for a relationship in which jealousy and uncertainty keep desire alive.

The speaker values felicitous poems as more important than great wealth and says that many women want to acquire a name through his poetry. He declares that only his mistress will be sung in his books and that she alone will provide the cause for his poetic talent. Love redirects his poetry from epic and tragedy toward the art of love and letters written for legendary figures.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: The poet encounters Elegy and Tragedy in a sacred grove, where they argue over the kind of poetry he should write. Tragedy urges him to abandon love poetry for heroic subjects, while Elegy defends her influence over the poet and over Corinna. The poet asks Tragedy to allow him time to continue writing about love, and Tragedy agrees. At a circus, the poet courts a woman who favors one of the charioteers, invokes Venus for success in love, and receives an encouraging smile and implied promise from the woman.

l: Ovid, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: The poet is visited in a sacred grove by Elegy and Tragedy, who debate whether he should continue writing love poetry or undertake a greater work. He persuades Tragedy to let him continue with short love poems for a while. At the circus, he addresses a woman at the races, praises her appearance, supports the charioteer she favors, and asks her to become his beloved.

l: Elegy, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: Elegy appears with one foot longer than the other, a graceful form, a thin robe, and a loving expression. She claims that she inspired the poet's work and taught Corinna to evade her guard and meet her lover. She argues that her light style is suited to Cupid and love, and she persuades the poet to continue writing in her manner.

l: Tragedy, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: Tragedy appears in a powerful stride, wearing a royal sceptre and a high Lydian buskin. She reproaches the poet for continually writing about love and urges him to sing of heroic deeds in a greater work. After the poet asks for more time, she grants permission for him to continue writing tender love poems.

l: love poetry, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: Love poetry is presented as the subject of the poet's earlier work and as a light form associated with Elegy and Cupid. Tragedy considers it too narrow for the poet's talent, while Elegy defends its power and influence. The poet is allowed to continue writing it temporarily before undertaking a greater task.

l: Cupid, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: Cupid is described by Elegy as light, like the poetry and subject associated with him. Elegy identifies herself as the companion and go-between of the goddess connected with sportive Love.

l: woman at the races, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: The woman at the races favors one of the charioteers, and the poet tries to win her favor while sitting beside her. He praises her legs and appearance, asks Venus to make her receptive to love, and interprets her smile and expressive eyes as a promise to grant him more elsewhere.

l: circus, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: The circus places the poet and the woman close together under its seating rules and provides the setting for the chariot race and the procession of the gods. Its crowd can demand that a race be restarted by waving their togas.

l: chariot race, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: The chariot race begins when the praetor releases four-horse teams from equally placed starting barriers. The poet supports the charioteer favored by the woman, worries when he loses ground, and urges the crowd to call for a restart. After the second start, the favored charioteer wins, while the poet says that his own desired prize remains to be won.

l: Venus, Heroides and Amores, LIBER TERTIUS
s: Venus is invoked during the procession of the gods as the goddess whom the poet and Cupid's powerful children applaud. The poet asks her to favor his efforts and to give his new mistress the disposition to endure being loved. Venus nods and gives a favorable sign.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The speaker complains that a faithless girl has broken her oath without losing her beauty, while the gods punish men but seem to tolerate beautiful women who swear falsely. He argues that guarding a wife cannot make her faithful, since desire is strengthened by prohibition, and advises the hard husband to indulge his wife instead. He then recounts a dream in which a white heifer is disturbed by a crow, leaves her bull, and joins other bulls, and the nocturnal dream augur interprets this as a sign of adultery. The unit presents beauty, female chastity, divine punishment, and forbidden desire as forces that shape human and divine behavior.

The speaker denounces the gods because the faithless girl has broken her oath yet remains beautiful, while he suffers for her wrongdoing. He argues that a woman's own character, rather than surveillance, must preserve her chastity, and he recounts a dream about a white heifer and a bull.

l: the speaker’s beloved woman, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The faithless girl swore falsely by her own eyes and by the speaker's eyes, but her appearance remains unchanged and beautiful. She is presented as deceiving both the speaker and, apparently, the gods without suffering punishment.

l: the gods, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The gods are accused of allowing beautiful women to swear falsely and of fearing to offend them. They punish men with Mars, Pallas, Apollo, and Jupiter's weapons, but Jupiter forbids his bolts to strike the fair forsworn.

l: the hard husband, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The hard husband places a keeper over his wife, but the speaker says that this achieves nothing because her will cannot be guarded. He is advised to abandon sternness, indulge his wife, and cultivate the friends she brings.

l: the wife, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The wife cannot be made faithful merely by having her body guarded, since her mind may remain unfaithful. Her beauty and the husband's concern for her make her more desirable to other men, and she may bring many friends into his social circle.

l: the white heifer, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The white heifer appears in the dream as the speaker's girl, with a dark mark left on her breast after a crow pecks her. She eventually leaves the bull and joins other bulls where the pasture is richer.

l: the bull, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The bull is the white heifer's happy mate and lies beside her while resting and chewing. After the heifer hesitates and leaves him, he is left on the abandoned bed.

l: the nocturnal dream augur, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The nocturnal dream augur interprets the speaker's dream by explaining each element. He identifies the heifer with the speaker's girl, the bull with the speaker, the crow with an old procuress, and the dark mark with evidence of adultery.

l: the dream vision, Heroides and Amores, III
s: The dream vision shows a grove, a green meadow, a white heifer with her bull, and a crow that pecks the heifer before she joins other bulls. Its interpretation presents the scene as a sign of the speaker's love, the girl's departure, and adultery.
Perjury occurs when the faithless girl breaks an oath sworn by her own eyes and by the speaker's eyes. The speaker complains that her perjury remains unpunished and that he suffers for it instead.

l: divine punishment, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Divine punishment is shown as falling on men and on figures such as Semele, while beautiful women who swear falsely appear protected. The speaker questions whether the gods exist or whether they favor tender beautiful women.

Beauty gives the faithless girl lasting privilege despite her false oath and makes the gods reluctant to offend her. It also increases the danger of jealousy and adultery because a guarded beautiful woman seems especially desirable.

l: marital fidelity and chastity, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Female chastity is genuine only when it remains after fear and external restraint have been removed. A woman who refrains from wrongdoing solely because she is forbidden to act is not considered truly chaste.

Adultery can occur despite locked doors and appointed guards because the mind and desire cannot be confined. In the dream interpretation, the dark mark on the heifer's breast indicates that her breast is not free from the stain of adultery.

l: guardianship of women, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Guardianship of women is presented as ineffective because a keeper can guard the body but not the will. The speaker says that strict custody provokes wrongdoing and that indulgence is a better way to influence a wife.

l: forbidden desire, Heroides and Amores, III
s: Forbidden desire makes people strive for what is denied and covet what is forbidden, like a sick person longing for prohibited water. The speaker uses the horse, Argus, Danae, and Penelope to show that restriction can intensify desire, while permission can weaken it.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The narrator hurries to reach his lady-love but is stopped by a swollen, unnamed river, which he reproaches for delaying him. He recalls rivers that aided or experienced love, especially Anio, who sees Ilia, rescues her from drowning, and takes her as his bride. The narrator then condemns the stream for being a muddy, temporary torrent and wishes it dry. In the next poem, he laments that poetry and the liberal arts have less value than military service and wealth, while a newly rich soldier is preferred to him.

The narrator is hurrying to reach his lady-love and asks the swollen river to stop its waters. When the river blocks his passage, he reproaches it, recalls the loves of other rivers, and later complains that wealth and military success are valued above his poetry.

The narrator's lady-love is the person he is trying to reach across the river. Elsewhere, she prefers a newly rich soldier to the narrator and keeps him from entering, while her guard and husband make access to her difficult.
Anio sees Ilia wandering barefoot and grieving beside his waters. He promises her refuge among his nymphs, rescues her when she throws herself into the river, and takes her as his bride.

Ilia wanders in distress because of her uncle's crime and Mars's wrongdoing, with her hair and cheeks marked by her nails. Fearing disgrace after being a Vestal, she throws herself into Anio's waters, which support her and make her his wife.

Love is presented as a force that makes rivers aid lovers or alter their courses. The narrator cites rivers such as Inachus, Xanthus, Alpheus, Peneus, Asopus, Achelous, Nile, Enipeus, and Anio as examples of rivers affected by love.

l: crossing the river, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The crossing is difficult because the river has no bridge or boat and has grown far deeper than it was before. The narrator cannot reach the farther bank by any art and is forced to stand waiting.

l: Ilia's drowning and marriage to Anio, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Ilia throws herself into the rushing waters after declaring that she would rather have died before becoming publicly disgraced. Anio is said to place his hands beneath her breast, keep her afloat, and share the rights of marriage with her.

l: poetry and the liberal arts, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The narrator asks whether anyone still respects the liberal arts or believes that delicate poetry brings any advantage. He contrasts poetic accomplishment with the military service and wealth that now win social preference.

l: the narrator's poems, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The narrator's poems have pleased his lady-love and earned her praise, but they do not secure him access to her. He is left outside her closed door despite the success of his books.

l: the newly rich soldier, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The newly rich soldier, whose wealth was gained through wounds and bloodshed, is preferred to the narrator. He has worn a helmet, carried a shield, borne a sword, and bears scars from earlier fighting.

War is treated as a more profitable pursuit than poetry because it can bring military rank and wealth. The narrator urges the wise to learn to follow battle and organize the foremost spears instead of merely producing good verse.

l: wealth and money, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Wealth and money are shown to control love, rank, public office, and social access. The narrator complains that those who can pay command his lady-love and that wealth gives weight to judges and status to knights.

Gold is described as more powerful than anything else because it can overcome resistance and purchase sexual access. The narrator also says that human beings dig gold from the earth instead of seeking agricultural abundance.

l: the poor, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The poor are excluded from the senate and deprived of the advantages that money provides. The narrator asks only that the wealthy leave something for poor lovers to win.

l: the rich, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: The rich possess the Campus and Forum and control peace, war, public honors, judgment, and romantic access. The narrator allows them to keep these privileges but objects when their greed takes away the loves of the poor.

l: human nature, Heroides and Amores, VI
s: Human nature is portrayed as ingenious but harmful to itself. It creates fortified cities, weapons, sea travel, and the pursuit of wealth instead of remaining content with the land and its natural gifts.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: The unit mourns Tibullus, whose death and funeral provoke grief from Elegy, Venus, Delia, Nemesis, his mother, and his sister, while poetry is presented as surviving the body and death. It argues that death can overcome the good and profane sacred things, though Tibullus may live on in poetic fame and in Elysium with other poets. The poem then describes Ceres’s festival and the goddess’s past love for Iasius, which once caused agriculture to fail everywhere except in Crete. Finally, the speaker declares his intention to escape a painful affair, but admits that love still conflicts with his hatred of his beloved woman and may continue to prevail.
Elegy is told to mourn Tibullus, loosen her hair, and weep because the singer and glory of her poetic strain has died. Her name is said to be all too truthful in this bereavement.

Tibullus is described as a sacred poet and a singer of Elegy. He dies and is burned on a high-reared funeral pyre, leaving only ashes for a small urn, but his poetic fame is expected to endure and he is imagined in Elysium.

Nemesis mourns Tibullus at his funeral and kisses him before not abandoning the pyre. She claims that Tibullus clung to her with failing strength as he died, and she is imagined as accompanying him in Elysium.

Delia comes to Tibullus’s funeral and kisses him with Nemesis and his family. As she descends from the pyre, she says that she was more happily loved by Tibullus and that he lived while she was his beloved.
Crete is presented as the land proud to have nurtured Jove. It alone remains fruitful when Ceres abandons the fields because of her love for Iasius.

Ceres is honored as the goddess who taught people to cultivate grain, use the sickle, yoke oxen, and turn the soil. During her love for Iasius, she neglects agriculture and causes the fields to fail except in Crete; her festival also separates the speaker from his beloved woman.
Bards are called sacred and the care of the gods, and some people believe that they possess divine power. Their work and poetic fame can survive death and fire.

The speaker mourns Tibullus, questions the usefulness of piety and the gods when good people die, and reflects on the endurance of poetry. In his own affair, he claims to have freed himself from love, yet admits that love and hatred struggle within him and that he may remain unable to stop loving.

l: the speaker’s beloved woman, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: The speaker’s beloved woman repeatedly rejects or deceives him, receives other lovers, and gives him false assurances. He resents her conduct but remains attracted to her beauty, which repeatedly draws him back.

Death is said to profane every sacred thing and to lay dark hands on all people, including poets and the pious. It drags the worshipper from the temple to the tomb and reduces Tibullus’s body to what a small urn can contain.

l: Tibullus’s funeral, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Tibullus’s funeral includes his burning on a pyre and the attendance of his mother, sister, Delia, and Nemesis. His mother closes his dying eyes, his sister shares the grief, and Delia and Nemesis offer kisses before the pyre is left.

l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Poetry alone is said to escape the greedy pyre. The fame of poetic works, including the renown of Troy and the story of the nightly woven and unwoven web, endures, allowing Tibullus, Nemesis, and Delia to remain known.

Love appears as a force that afflicts both mortals and gods, including Ceres’s love for Iasius. The speaker tries to reject love, but his attraction to his beloved woman’s beauty overcomes his hatred of her faults.

l: Ceres’s festival, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Ceres’s annual festival requires the speaker’s beloved woman to remain alone in a separate bed. The speaker objects that a festival should welcome love, songs, and wine rather than impose separation.

l: grain and agriculture, Heroides and Amores, IX
s: Ceres teaches the cultivation, harvesting, and plowing of grain, replacing earlier foods such as acorns and turf herbs. When she abandons the fields for love, crops fail across the land, while Crete remains fertile and even the wild boar is said to reap grain there.

l: Heroides and Amores, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid says that his books of verse have made Corinna known to many and have turned her into a woman shared by others. He asks Corinna to conceal her infidelity and deny what he sees, because discovering or hearing her confess her affairs causes him intense distress. The poems also describe Falerii’s annual rites to Juno and trace them to Halaesus, while Ovid celebrates Sulmo and his Paelignian origin. In another episode, Ovid suffers sexual impotence with a willing girl, despite having recently performed successfully with Chlide, Pitho, Libas, and Corinna.

Corinna is the woman whom Ovid alone began to love, but he fears that she must now be shared with many. Ovid says that she alone stirred his poetic genius and that his praise of her beauty has made her known and sexually available to others.

Ovid blames his poetry for making Corinna common and regrets having praised her beauty. He identifies himself as a Paelignian poet from Sulmo, celebrates his literary reputation, and ends his elegies while turning toward the greater subject associated with Lyaeus.

l: Ovid's books of verse, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid's books of verse have made Corinna known beyond their private relationship. They have therefore helped turn her into a woman who may be shared with many and have harmed Ovid's interests.

l: Ovid's poetry, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid's poetry is said to have stirred his genius through Corinna and to have caused her beauty to be publicly advertised. He also presents poetry as capable of creating or transmitting marvelous myths, without being bound by historical truth.
Halaesus fled his homeland after Agamemnon was killed, wandering over land and sea before founding the walls of Falerii. He taught the Faliscans the rites of Juno.

Falerii is associated with an annual festival of Juno involving priestesses, games, processions, offerings, and animal sacrifices. Its Juno rites are said to have been brought by Halaesus, and Ovid wishes the goddess to remain friendly to Falerii and its people.
Sulmo is Ovid's watery hometown, whose walls enclose only a few acres of plain. Ovid imagines a stranger praising the small town for having produced so great a poet.

l: love affair and infidelity, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid fears that Corinna, formerly regarded as his own, is now involved with many men. He remains attached to her despite jealousy and asks her to continue her affairs privately rather than force him to know or witness them.

l: fame and public reputation, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Public reputation is presented as depending on whether a woman's faults are exposed or denied. Ovid urges Corinna to appear modest in public, conceal her sexual conduct, and allow him to enjoy the mistaken belief that she is faithful.

l: concealment and denial, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid asks Corinna to deny her affairs even when the evidence is visible, promising that his eyes will yield to her words. He considers being deceived a kind of duty and says that a simple denial can make her victorious over him.

l: Ovid's Paelignian homeland, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid identifies himself as a child of the Paelignian countryside and predicts that he will be called the glory of the Paelignian people. He links that people with the honorable arms they took up when Rome feared its allied forces.

l: sexual impotence, Heroides and Amores, XII
s: Ovid experiences sexual impotence with a beautiful and willing girl, despite her embraces, kisses, words, and efforts to arouse him. He wonders whether magic, poison, or shame has caused the failure, and contrasts it with his recent success with Chlide, Pitho, Libas, and Corinna.

The document is a sequence of elegiac love letters and love poems attributed to P. Ovidius Naso. It begins with Heroides, letters in which women, and later men, address absent, faithless, endangered, or desired partners. Its central concerns are separation, betrayal, erotic desire, marriage, abandonment, danger, and the destructive pressure of love. The Heroides opens with Penelope’s faithful appeal to Ulysses amid intrusive suitors, then moves through complaints and pleas by Phyllis, Briseis, Phaedra, Oenone, Hypsipyle, Dido, Hermione, Deianira, Ariadne, Canace, Medea, Laodamia, Hypermestra, and Sappho. These writers recall promises, wars, forced marriages, rival women, lost homes, children, and impending death; several threaten or resolve upon suicide. The sequence also includes exchanges: Paris pursues Helen, while Helen resists yet admits attraction and fear; Leander and Hero long to meet across dangerous waters; and Acontius seeks to enforce Cydippe’s oath, while Cydippe condemns his deceit before yielding to the bond that Diana appears to enforce. The document then introduces Amores, presented as a reduced collection of three books. In Liber Primus, Cupid turns the poet from epic into elegy. The speaker pursues a beloved woman, especially Corinna, through secret messages, banquets, closed doors, sexual encounters, quarrels, and refusals. Dipsas instructs a girl to exploit wealthy lovers, while the poet insists that poetry, service, and devotion should matter more than payment. Liber Secundus expands the unstable lover’s world: he claims to be unable to resist women, suspects and commits infidelity, mourns Corinna’s parrot, loves two women at once, fears Corinna’s sea voyage and pregnancy, sends a ring, and argues about jealousy, guardianship, and poetic vocation. Love repeatedly diverts him from epic and tragedy. In Liber Tertius, Elegy and Tragedy debate the poet’s future, but he continues erotic poetry. The poems treat false oaths, adultery, jealous husbands, delays caused by a river, the low social value of poetry, Tibullus’s death and poetic survival, painful attachment, Corinna’s public notoriety, local cult and homeland, and the speaker’s sexual failure. Across the whole document, letters and poems portray love as compelling, creative, comic, jealous, and often fatal.

Penelope, daughter of Icarius and mother of Telemachus, faithfully awaits Ulysses amid loneliness and suitors. She preserves herself, uses her web to beguile them, writes Ulysses seeking his return, and finally tests young men with the bow.

Odysseus, also called Ulysses, survives the Trojan War and Troy’s fall as a victor, remembered for a night attack and Troy’s destruction. Returning remains uncertain: he is absent from Penelope, father to Telemachus, and carries Aeolus’s wind skins and a plow for ruined Troy.

Troy is a Phrygian, Neptunian Pergamum: Priam’s kingdom and a royal city of high towers, strong walls, temples, wealth, and crowded people. Paris, restored there as a royal child, is celebrated at its festivals; he imagines bringing Helen there with rich garments, textiles, and gold. Helen acknowledges its wealth and population but calls it barbarous, fearing separation from her family, judgment by Priam’s household, and reproach from Dardanian wives. Cassandra warns that Paris’s departure will bring flames, and prophecy marks Troy for destruction by fire. It becomes the enemy city sought by the Danaans, destination of their fleet, and site of the Trojan War, feared by Laodamia for the dangers awaiting Protesilaus. In the end Troy falls, burns, and is reduced to ashes; returning Greeks take Trojan spoil, while crops and grass cover its ruins and the bones of the dead.
Telemachus, son of Ulysses and Penelope, seeks news of Ulysses at Pylos, learns from Nestor of Ulysses’s Trojan War deeds, reports them to Penelope, and survives an attempt on his life.
Laertes, an aged, powerless defender of Penelope's household and Ulysses's father, urges Penelope to leave widowhood, but her fidelity and prayers temper him.
Suitors from Dulichium, Samos, and Zacynthus crowd into Ulysses's hall, seek Penelope, and during his absence consume and spoil his possessions as masters.
Paris's brother and Andromache's husband, Hector is praised as a warrior and Trojan strength, then a lamented hero dragged by Haemonian horses.

Achilles is a great captain, warrior, and hero, son of Peleus and a seaborn goddess, father of Pyrrhus, and master and husband of Briseis. He possesses a sword, the Pelian spear, and a lyre. After taking and loving Briseis, he withdraws from fighting, plays the lyre, plans to leave Phthia, and refuses appeals to restore her while Hector attacks the Danaans. Briseis urges his return to battle.

Paris is a Phrygian and Priamid, son and descendant of Priam, of the royal line and descended through ancestry from Jupiter and Laomedon. He recalls an earlier life as a poor slave and shepherd on Ida, husband to Oenone; after his recognition as Priam’s son, he abandons her and later has a new wife. He presents himself as noble, wealthy, handsome, youthful, and skilled with weapons, archery, horses, and contests, possessing ships, men, and the strength for war. His defining divine role is judge of Venus, Juno, and Minerva. He prefers Helen to the gifts of Juno and Pallas, receives Helen as the alleged prize of the judgment, and is characterized as better suited to Venus than Mars. Paris then writes to Helen and undertakes a voyage to Lacedaemon. As a Trojan guest and stranger in Menelaus’s household, he openly and secretly pursues Helen while she is married: looking at and signaling to her, sharing her drinking place, sending declarations of love, offering gifts, and urging a secret meeting during Menelaus’s absence. Helen finds him handsome, persuasive, and daring, but also rash, immodest, late, and possibly untrustworthy. He is accused of violating hospitality and entering as a guest but acting as an enemy. He commands a prepared Trojan fleet, travels from Lacedaemon, and carries Helen away. His passion for her is steadfast, yet Oenone accuses him of choosing a stolen wife over his homeland and former love, while others call him a beautiful but faithless guest and a lover who took Menelaus’s wife.
The gods, divine beings feared by men, are condemned for fearing beautiful women, permitting their false oaths, and punishing men with divine weapons while sparing fair perjurers.
Danaans sail a thousand ships toward Troy to wage the Trojan War over Menelaus’s stolen wife, despite winds and Laodamia’s plea to spare Protesilaus, returning victorious commanders.
Trojans, a wealthy, populous group in Asia, fight Argives in the Trojan War and prepare to welcome Helen with gifts, ceremonies, and honor.
Thrace is a place containing Rhodope, ruled by Phyllis; she gives Demophoon Lycurgus's realms there, and its people will not marry her for preferring a foreigner.

The Trojan War is a war between Greece and Troy, fought for Helen, the abducted wife whom Menelaus demands back. It begins in the threat created by Paris's choice to take Helen: hostile arms seek her return, and Helen herself foresees Menelaus, her brothers, and Tyndareus answering in anger. Paris imagines either taking her without fighting or resisting the Greeks with Troy, Asia, horses, weapons, and Hector. The conflict brings persistent fear and grief to those awaiting the fighters, including Penelope and Laodamia. In the fighting, Ulysses joins the killings of Rhesus and Dolon and a night attack on the Thracian camp; Achilles refuses to fight while Hector harms the Danaan forces, until Briseis urges Achilles to return to battle. The war ends in Troy's destruction, Menelaus's victory and return, and the separation and captivity of survivors, including Hermione's vulnerability to Pyrrhus.

l: the burning of Troy, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a destruction [leaving Troy in ashes] The fall of Troy brings the Greek leaders home and leads to sacrifices, offerings, and the display of Trojan spoils. Although Troy has fallen, Penelope gains little comfort because Ulysses remains away.
Penelope declares that she remains Ulysses's wife and will always be called Penelope, the wife of Ulysses. She refuses to leave her widowed bed despite her father's pressure and the suitors' demands.

Ulysses's prolonged absence causes Penelope to fear every danger of land and sea and even to suspect that he may be held by another love. His absence also allows the suitors to dominate his household and endanger Telemachus.
Penelope writes and sends Ulysses a letter by any traveler, seeking reliable news of him and asking its recipient to deliver it if he is seen.

l: the suitors' threat, Heroides and Amores
s: The suitors threaten Penelope’s marriage, Ulysses’s household and resources, oppress Penelope, and endanger Telemachus through an attempted ambush during his planned journey to Pylos.

Phyllis, a Thracian queen and Demophoon’s hostess, faithfully loves and aids him with refuge, gifts, and her virginity. Deceived by his promises and absence, she watches for his return, reproaches him, and despairingly contemplates suicide.
Demophoon, Phyllis’s guest, accepts her hospitality, aid, gifts, love, and trust, promises marriage and return, then remains absent, apparently having another wife.
is_a mountain [shaded and icy] Rhodope is the region where Phyllis received Demophoon and ruled broad realms. It is described as icy and extending toward Haemus.

Theseus is a person: son of Neptune and Aethra, husband of Phaedra, and father of Hippolytus. He slays the Minotaur, kills Hippolytus’s mother, abandons Ariadne despite a marriage pledge, and abducts Helen. Ariadne reproaches his betrayal after he leaves her asleep and sails away. Later, while absent with Pirithous, Phaedra says he prefers Pirithous, neglects their marriage, and has harmed her family.

Ariadne is a woman who aids Theseus with a thread, then awakens abandoned on an island after his departure. Alone, threatened by wild beasts, injured and fearful of stranger-men, she searches the shore, calls to him, and signals his ship with her veil. She fears exile and an unburied death, begs to be remembered, and later is married to Bacchus.

Venus is a sea-born goddess of love and beauty, mother of Aeneas and Cupid, and beloved of Mars; she is also involved with Mars in an adulterous affair. She wins Paris's judgment among three goddesses through her beauty and her promise that he will possess Helen, later sponsoring his marriage to her on a painted ship. Helen both doubts Venus's praise and is pleased by it. Venus rules in the city of Aeneas, favors a young woman after Mars departs, and is invoked by Dipsas to excuse deception and false oaths in love. Though linked to love's camp, she and Cupid are described as unwarlike and unsuited to soldiers' pay. Speakers invoke her to grant or permit love, distinguish her powers from Minerva's, and favor poetic love; in a procession she nods and gives a favorable sign for a new mistress to endure being loved.

The sea is a body of water and a dangerous realm, tossed by wind and wave, bordering Phyllis at her coast and harbor. It matters most as a treacherous barrier and threat to travelers, ships, and sailors: stormy, deep, and raging, with contrary winds, rocks, Scylla, Charybdis, the Syrtes, and the Ceraunian mountains. It keeps Demophoon from Phyllis, surrounds Ariadne’s island, and may punish faithlessness and broken promises. From watched waters and delayed return, it unfolds into fears of shipwreck, isolation, rough waves, and death as the shore recedes.
Demophoon's damaged ships are refitted by Phyllis, supplied with oars, depart her harbor, never return, and prompt her mistaken sightings.
Demophoon swears by divine witnesses, marriage rites, and the sea to return and honor promises, but Phyllis later questions the vanished oaths and pledged hand.
Marriage is promised to Phyllis as a lasting bond and assurance with Demophoon, but she regrets it and fears he has another wife.

is_caused_by Demophoon [according to the proposed tomb inscription] Phyllis says that Demophoon will be named on her tomb as the cause of her death. She declares that he will have caused it, while she herself will have supplied the hand.
Betrayed, deceived, and abandoned by Demophoon, Phyllis contemplates suicide, considering drowning in the bay, poison, a sword, or a noose without delay.

Briseis, a captive woman from Lyrnesus and Achilles’ beloved slave, loses her husband and three brothers when her homeland is destroyed. Taken captive by Achilles, she is later removed from him. In grief she writes to accuse him of not reclaiming her, recounts her losses, and begs him to take her back or let her die, offering humble service in Phthia.
Agamemnon, king of the Greeks, demands Briseis, causing anger; he later regrets it, seeks Achilles’ reconciliation with gifts and marriage, and is attracted to Cassandra.

Pyrrhus, Achilles’ son and an Aeacides, possesses his father’s arms and is said to have killed Aegisthus; promised Hermione, he holds her captive and takes her to his palace against her refusal, becoming her marital oppressor and Orestes’ target of blame.
Lesbian women, including unmarried and married proles, are sea-daughters named by the Aeolian lyre who come to hear Sappho; loved by her despite reproach, they are asked to stop until Phaon returns.

Briseis's captivity began when Achilles destroyed Lyrnesus, killed her husband and brothers, and captured her. Taken from Achilles and delivered to Agamemnon, she fears abandonment or transfer; it may end if Achilles orders her return.

Achilles' anger began with Agamemnon's taking of Briseis and has kept him from fighting for the Danaans. Briseis asks him to conquer his anger, since Agamemnon now regrets his own wrath and Greece lies distressed before him. She wants her return to be both the cause and the end of his anger.
Briseis’s tear-blotted Greek letter to Achilles complains of his delay, recalls her suffering, repeatedly asks him to reclaim her, and ends by asking whether to come as captive or servant.

Phaedra, a Cretan maid, Minos and Pasiphae’s daughter, Ariadne’s sister, and Theseus’s wife, is seized by late, intense love for Hippolytus. Love wounds her, strips her modesty, and draws her to hunting. She writes and confesses, invoking her lineage, criticizing Theseus, and begging Hippolytus to accept her.
Hippolytus is a heroic Amazon-born man: a vigorous, stern, handsome hunter devoted to Diana, praised for riding and weapons yet defined by iron-hearted resistance to Phaedra’s plea for love.

Cupid is a winged god of love, Venus’s brother and Mars’s stepson, armed with bow, arrows, quiver, and even a thunderbolt. He rules love with changeable but commanding power, described as light and sportive while also able to burn, wound, deceive, conquer, and frustrate lofty aims. He commands Phaedra to write to Hippolytus, kindles her fierce passion, overcomes her modesty, and is said to rule even the gods. With his mother, he laughs at a lover’s old fear, promises courage, and remains beside the lover at a guarded door. Cupid has his own camp, in which every lover serves as a soldier; though he wounds a faithful speaker, that speaker finally invites him and his mother to reign in the speaker’s heart. Love also defeats the speaker’s epic and tragic ambitions, leading the poet away from tragedy in triumph, while making unequal partners fit together. In the end, his force extends to rivers, causing them to aid lovers or alter their courses.
Phaedra’s letter to Hippolytus carries secrets across land and sea, confesses love when speech failed, praises him, attacks Theseus, proposes union, and ends tearfully pleading forgiveness.

l: Theseus and Phaedra’s marriage, Heroides and Amores
s: Theseus and Phaedra’s marriage is a marital covenant threatened by Phaedra’s love. Though she says she would not break it or stain her reputation, she claims Theseus neglects it and urges a disguised union with Hippolytus.

Crete, a land of a hundred cities, is known for nurturing the infant Jupiter or Jove. Ariadne cannot return after betraying her father and homeland for Theseus; later, Crete alone remains fertile when Ceres abandons other fields.
Minos is identified as Ariadne’s father. Ariadne says that her father and his realm were betrayed by her actions when she helped Theseus escape.

Diana is a maiden goddess of Delos, daughter of Leto and sister of Apollo, associated with hunting, the bow, and quiver. Present in her temple when Cydippe read Acontius’s oath, she witnesses, records, and acknowledges the pledge, making her a binding divine witness to the promised marriage. Acontius invokes her as a powerful, violent avenger who may punish Cydippe for breaking faith and who favors him beyond what seems just. Cydippe interprets her continuing illness and failed marriages as Diana’s anger, despite offerings of incense and sacrifice at her shrine. Diana is also said to be able to restore Cydippe’s health, and Cydippe asks her to relent and seek Apollo’s healing aid.

Aurora, dawn and Tithonus’s wife, loves Cephalus and mothers Memnon; she crosses the ocean from her aged husband in a golden chariot, bringing day despite complaints she disrupts lovers, workers, and students.

Ceres is a goddess of grain, fertility, and agriculture, honored for teaching people cultivation, sickles, oxen, and soil-turning. She governs crops and makes Crete fertile, but her love for Iasius overcomes shame and leads her to neglect agriculture, causing fields to fail except in Crete.

l: marital fidelity and chastity, Heroides and Amores
s: Marital fidelity and chastity are presented as enduring, voluntary moral commitments. Oenone contrasts her faithfulness with Helen’s alleged infidelity and warns that violated chastity cannot be restored; Helen calls fidelity sacred and protects her honor; the final record defines genuine chastity as restraint freely maintained without fear or external prohibition.

Oenone is a fountain nymph, celebrated in the Phrygian forests and daughter of a great river. Paris’s formerly loved, faithful wife, she possesses healing herbs and is loved by Faunus. Abandoned when Paris returns with Helen, she writes grieving, condemning his new marriage, and begging him to return.

Helen is a woman of Spartan and Taenarian identity, born in rural Therapnae and from Eurotas, daughter of Leda, a Tyndarid, and descendant of Tyndareus, Pelops, and Tantalus. She is Menelaus’s lawful wife, initially marked by marital fidelity, virtue, chastity, a blameless reputation, and Menelaus’s trust. Previously abducted by Theseus against her will, she remained untouched and was attended by Aethra and Clymene. Her exceptional beauty makes her, to Paris, the greatest prize and the object of a desire that began before he saw her; Venus favors her and promises her to Paris. When Paris arrives in Lacedaemon, he presses her to become his wife, meet him secretly, and join him in Ilion, where he predicts royal, almost divine honors. Helen condemns his betrayal of hospitality and defends her honor, though she admits his attractiveness and the effect of his attention. She remains fearful and undecided, weighing desire against disgrace, abandonment, violence, and separation from family and support. Oenone later calls her an adulteress, says Paris brought her to Troy, and doubts her fidelity; she is carried from Eurotas in a Phrygian ship and promised a royal welcome in Ilion.

Menelaus is Helen’s husband and a king whose far-reaching authority continues to guard her while he is away in Crete on a cause seen as great and just. He trusts Helen’s morals and way of life, allowing her freedom, yet she fears betraying him and being noticed for concealed signals with Paris. Paris calls him Helen’s absent present husband and contests his superiority in beauty, age, courage, and military ability.

l: Paris's new wife, Heroides and Amores
s: Paris’s new Greek wife arrives by ship clinging to him, portrayed by Oenone as an unfaithful rival who abandoned her husband and will bring danger to Paris and Troy.
Xanthus is Oenone’s river, preserving her and Paris’s memory; after his desertion, she calls its waters backward toward its fountain.
Oenone’s letter to Paris asks whether he will read it, recalls their bond, voices grief and accusations, warns him, and pleads for his return.

l: the ship carrying Paris, Heroides and Amores
s: carries Helen [on Paris's return] The ship is built from felled firs and hewn timbers, receives its waxed sails, and carries Paris away. Oenone later recognizes its sails, sees Helen aboard, and watches it reach the shore.

Marriage preparations have been made for the speaker three times, but each ceremony has failed when her illness and fear of death appear. The speaker ultimately presents union with Acontius as the remaining course.
